title: Triratna
hookLine: a Western Buddhist community founded in 1967

cards: A woman walks into an ordination ceremony with the name her parents gave her, and walks out with a new one, a Sanskrit name her aunt will mispronounce at dinner for years.
A simple stole now hangs around her neck for ceremonies. On Monday she'll be back at work as a nurse, and Monday night she'll cook for her kids. She hasn't become a nun.
She has joined an order, and that difference sits near the heart of her community.

teach.h: AN ENGLISH MONK BACK FROM INDIA.
teach.b: First, the founder. Triratna was started in Britain by an Englishman known as Sangharakshita.
Born Dennis Lingwood in London, he spent many years in India as a Buddhist monk, studying with teachers from several traditions.
Back in Britain, he found people eager to practice and started a new community for them, which grew into what is now the Triratna Buddhist Community. Second, the name.
Triratna is Sanskrit for the three jewels: the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, the community. Going for refuge to those three is at the center of the whole movement. Third, the big idea.
Triratna has an order, and people are ordained into it with a new name. But the order is neither monks nor laypeople in the old sense.

Its saying: commitment is primary, lifestyle secondary. A member may be married or single, may live in a shared house with other members or alone, may work an ordinary job or in one of the community's own businesses.
What makes someone a member is going for refuge, not what they wear or where they sleep.
The community draws freely on teachings from different Buddhist traditions, and on Western poetry and art too. Fourth, the hard part. A new community has no centuries of habit to steady it.
Triratna has had to face painful accounts from former members about its founder's conduct and about harm in its early years, and it has published its own responses.
Building something new means building, too, the ways to face what went wrong.

how: Members of the Triratna Buddhist Community go for refuge to the three jewels; those ordained into its order receive a new name and may be married or single, living in shared communities or alone, under the principle that commitment is primary and lifestyle secondary.

games.q: you're Sangharakshita, home in Britain after years in India. people want to practice deeply, but few will become monks. what do you build?
o: a monastery, and only monks may truly join.
an order where commitment comes first and lifestyle second.
a lecture series with no community at all.
games.why: an order of committed members who may be married or single, at home or in shared houses: going for refuge, not robes, is what makes a member.

practice: Bring to mind one community you know that's younger than you, or close to it: a congregation, a club, a support group, even a group chat.

Ask quietly what holds its people together, not the logo or the rules but the thing they keep coming back for, and what it would need to admit, forgive and protect to stay healthy a long time, and breathe with those questions.
If someone is hurting you or you're in danger, reach out: 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Triratna. Sanskrit for the three jewels, and the name of a Western Buddhist community founded by Sangharakshita, whose order puts commitment before lifestyle. Today's word.
